sections.html:
• Genus of rheophyte plants from the banks of fast-moving streams in Borneo.
  • Easy to care for; tolerates low to medium light and needs no substrate.
  • Very slow growing and more expensive than anubias.
  • Height: 5–10 cm for creeping types, 18–25 cm for upright types; leaves 1–10 cm long.

Bucephalandra is relatively new to the aquarium hobby and in high demand, and it grows very slowly compared to other species, so it costs more than anubias. As plant farms gradually increase their stock, prices should fall over time.

To help prevent overharvesting in the wild, farm-raised plants are preferable.
Bucephalandra grows along the banks of fast-moving streams in Borneo. It grows emersed (above water) during the dry season and submersed (below water) during the rainy season.
Because of their native habitat in fast-moving rivers, bucephalandra have developed very strong roots, so they do well in tanks with high flow once established.

Some species grow by creeping horizontally and stay around 5–10 cm tall, whereas upright species may reach 18–25 cm. Leaves range from 1–10 cm long. The plant is often used in the foreground or middle of the aquarium, or attached to hardscape, and suits nano aquariums.

Buce are considered easy to care for: they can live in low light, do not need much fertilizer or CO2 injection, and can grow without any substrate. They grow very slowly and can be prone to algae, so growing them in shaded parts of the tank and using algae eaters to keep the leaves clean helps. Higher light may invite algae problems because of their slow growth.

Planting

Like anubias and java fern, buce have a rhizome, a thick stem that sprouts both leaves and roots. They do not need to be planted in substrate. Wedge them into a crack in a rock or attach them to decor with sewing thread or super glue gel. Do not smother the rhizome with too much glue.

If planting in the substrate, the rhizome must not be covered. Push the plant deep into sand or gravel so the roots and rhizome are buried, then gently pull it upwards until the rhizome is completely exposed but the roots remain in the substrate.

Another option is to leave the plant in its plastic basket with rock wool. Feed it by inserting a root tab into the rock wool so that it reaches the roots.

Melting

Most plant farms grow their plants emersed, so when a new buce is submerged, some leaves may melt while it adjusts. Nutrients are stored mainly in the rhizome, so do not throw it away. As long as the rhizome looks healthy, leave it in the aquarium and it will grow new shoots that form leaves and roots.

Fertilizer

Like most rhizome plants, buce take most of their nutrients from the water column and benefit from an all-in-one liquid fertilizer.

Emersed growth

Buce do well grown emersed, for example in a paludarium or terrarium with plenty of water and high humidity. They can be grown together with moss to keep their roots moist at all times.

Buce have care requirements very similar to anubias and java fern and handle a wide range of temperatures, 21–28°C, and pH 6–8. They grow in low to medium light. Adding CO2 is not necessary, but it can speed up growth.

In the wild, buce usually produce flowers above water with special odours that attract pollinators. Successful fertilisation results in fruit with seeds that drop into the water and spread to other areas. Flowers grown underwater are beautiful but do not produce seeds.

In an aquarium, the easiest way to propagate buce is to cut the rhizome into two pieces with clean, sharp scissors, ideally at a natural bend where the plant has begun to form separate clumps of foliage. Attach the new piece to a rock or driftwood and it will continue growing as a second plant.

Bucephalandra has oblong leaves with wavy edges, though some types are rounder, narrower or have straight edges. Foliage varies from light to dark green, and some varieties have red, purple or bluish tints. Some species have small white dots on the leaves and an iridescent sheen that changes in the light. A thriving plant may produce a white or pink flower.

More than 30 species have been identified, but there are hundreds of trade names, such as green wavy, brownie blue, black pearl, mini coin, dark skeleton king, Godzilla and deep purple.
